    All You Need in One Device

    By a click of a button, stairs’ height and slope’s degree can be easily adjusted to meets patients’ current abilities and needs.

    DPE Medical Wins Top Rehabilitation Solution of 2025!

    Learn more

    DST Triple Models

    are a multi-functional, adjustable platforms, that provide a safe environment for full gait rehabilitation, including:

    Adjustable Stair Practice

    Adjustable Stair Practice

    The device includes four height-adjustable stairs, enabling a gradual and safe progression from low step practice to full stair climbing—matching each patient’s abilities and stage of recovery.
    height range: 0-16.5cm,

    0-6.5 inches

    3m/10feet Parallel bars

    3m/10feet Parallel bars

    In its flat position, the device replaces outdated parallel bars with a sleek, fully electric handrail system — offering smooth, height-adjustable support for safer, more dynamic gait and balance training, with minimal setup and maximum clinical flexibility.

    Adjustable Slope Practice

    Adjustable Slope Practice

    The device includes a fully adjustable slope, enabling controlled and progressive training on inclines—from flat walking to challenging uphill simulations. This allows therapists to tailor the difficulty to each patient’s current functional level.
    slope range: 0-26 degrees

    Electric Parallel Bars

    Adjustable Staircase & Slope

    Full Gait Rehabilitation, one device

    DST for Children
    The DST can be used by children as young as four years old. Learn how to better adjust your DST for the use of children
    Why practice stairs?
    Institutions may benefit greatly from stair training programs because they can challenge a patient's strength, range of motion, and cardiovascular ability better than practice plane walking.

    Conducting Clinical Studies with the DST

    For a full list of articles click here​

    The DST’s unique abilities and easy adjustment can eliminate well-known research limitations. For example, by adjusting the height of the stairs and handrails to patients’ current physical abilities, some comparison can be made between patients with different physical abilities, such as their mechanical efficiency during stair climbing. Patients’ mechanical efficiency, measured through physiological parameters, is a predictor for mechanical efficiency in other functions, such as ambulation, and thus holds great value to the rehabilitation process.
